common_name: Mishirasu Asian Pear (Hokkaido Giant Russet Pear)

planting.note: Plant a bare-root or grafted tree while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained soil; selected on Hokkaido in the late 1800s and is among the largest-fruited Asian pear cultivars, so it benefits from fruit thinning to one per cluster to reach full size. Plant a second Asian pear cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Mishirasu produces some of the largest fruit of any nashi cultivar, often exceeding a pound, with russet brown-gold skin and crisp, juicy, sweet flesh eaten fresh rather than cooked, unlike soft European pears. It stores unusually well for an Asian pear. Like most nashi cultivars it is not self-fertile and needs a different Pyrus pyrifolia cultivar blooming at the same time for a full crop, and it carries the fire blight susceptibility typical of most Asian pear varieties.

planting.note: Plant bare-root while dormant in late winter in full sun and well-drained soil; the earliest-ripening nashi cultivar commonly sold in North America, typically harvested in early August, well ahead of Hosui and Chojuro. Plant with another Asian pear cultivar for cross-pollination.

directions: Hamese bears medium-size, yellow-skinned fruit that is the first Asian pear to ripen in many home orchards, with crisp, crunchy, very juicy flesh and a refreshingly sweet, mild flavor unlike the soft, buttery texture of European pears. Because it is not self-fertile, plant it near a different Asian pear cultivar with overlapping bloom for reliable fruit set, and watch for fire blight, to which most nashi cultivars remain susceptible.
sources: NW Fruit (Western Washington Fruit Research Foundation)

planting.note: Plant bare-root while dormant in late winter; a Chinese-origin Asian pear that blooms 10-14 days earlier than Bartlett, so choose a planting site with good air drainage to reduce spring frost risk to the early blossoms. Cross-pollinate with a different Asian pear cultivar.

directions: Seuri produces round, medium-size fruit with yellow-brown skin and crisp flesh that is sweet with a touch of tartness and a hint of apricot, considered by growers to be among the most flavorful of the nashi pears rather than the milder taste typical of many Asian pear cultivars. Its unusually early bloom time is its most distinctive trait and requires a compatible cross-pollinator flowering in the same window. As with most Asian pears, fruit is picked crisp and eaten fresh rather than ripened off the tree, and the tree is generally susceptible to fire blight.

planting.note: Plant bare-root while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; needs a different Asian pear cultivar nearby for cross-pollination and reliable fruit set.

directions: Meigetsu is a pleasantly sweet Japanese nashi cultivar with fruit and aroma often compared to pineapple, watermelon, and butterscotch. Unlike most nashi pears prized for a hard, crunchy bite, Meigetsu's flesh is comparatively soft, giving it a texture closer to a ripe European pear while still being harvested and eaten fresh rather than after a storage ripening period. It is not self-fertile and, like other Asian pear cultivars, is vulnerable to fire blight in humid climates.

planting.note: Plant bare-root while dormant in late winter; a productive, mid-to-early season nashi cultivar typically ripening in early September. Plant with a different Asian pear cultivar for cross-pollination.

directions: Ichiban Nashi produces fine-textured, crisp fruit with a mellow butterscotch flavor, eaten fresh rather than cooked or stored to soften the way European pears are. The tree is noted for reliable, heavy production once established. It requires a compatible cross-pollinator and, in common with most nashi cultivars, offers little inherent resistance to fire blight.
sources: NW Fruit (Western Washington Fruit Research Foundation)

common_name: Ooharabeni Asian Pear (Red-Blushed Japanese Hybrid Pear)

planting.note: Plant bare-root while dormant in late winter; a compact interspecific hybrid bred by Japan's NARO Institute of Fruit Tree Science from a Red Bartlett x Asian pear cross, and it needs a different pear cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Ooharabeni is an unusual cross between European Red Bartlett and an Asian pear parent, ripening red-blushed, medium, round fruit in late August to early September with a flavor sweeter and more aromatic than typical nijisseiki-type nashi pears. Its compact tree opens with red spring foliage that turns green by summer, and the fruit is noted for good resistance to scab. Like other Asian pear-type cultivars, fruit is best picked and eaten crisp rather than ripened further in storage.

common_name: Mount Vernon Asian Pear (WSU Research Station Selection)

planting.note: Plant bare-root while dormant in late winter; selected from open-pollinated Asian pear seedlings at the WSU Mount Vernon research station and is well suited to the cool, short-summer maritime Pacific Northwest where many other nashi cultivars fail to ripen fully. Plant a second Asian pear cultivar nearby for pollination.

directions: Mount Vernon was identified by Raintree Nursery as the best of many open-pollinated Asian pear seedlings trialed at the Washington State University Mount Vernon Northwestern Washington Research and Extension Station, making it a Pacific Northwest regional selection bred for maritime climates. It bears large, round, cream-colored fruit in mid-season with crisp, juicy flesh and excellent flavor, eaten fresh rather than stored to soften. It is not self-fertile and needs a compatible Asian pear cultivar for cross-pollination.
sources: NW Fruit (Western Washington Fruit Research Foundation)

common_name: Dangshan Su Li Asian Pear (Chinese White Pear)

planting.note: Plant bare-root while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained soil; a traditional Chinese white pear from Dangshan County, Anhui Province, and needs a different Pyrus cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Dangshan Su Li is one of China's most widely grown white pear cultivars, native to Dangshan County, a region long known for large-scale pear production. Its smooth golden-yellow skin covers crisp, juicy, mildly sweet flesh eaten fresh at harvest, unlike the soft-ripening habit of European pears. As a Pyrus bretschneideri cultivar it needs a compatible cross-pollinator and, like most Asian pear species, has limited natural resistance to fire blight.

common_name: Tennosui Asian Pear (Fire Blight-Resistant Texas Pear)

planting.note: Plant bare-root while dormant in late winter; needs only about 400 chill hours, making it well suited to the Gulf South and other warm-winter regions, and it is self-fertile so a second cultivar is not required for fruit set, though yields improve with a pollinator nearby.

directions: Tennosui was bred from a cross of the Tennessee pear and Hosui Asian pear by a Harris County, Texas extension horticulturist and released by Texas A&M in 2004 specifically for humid, fire blight-prone regions of the South. Its bell-shaped fruit ripens early, from late July into August, with crisp flesh that resists browning after cutting, a trait growers value for fresh eating. Unlike many nashi cultivars, Tennosui shows notably good field resistance to fire blight, and it is self-fertile, though cross-pollination with another pear cultivar can improve crop size.

planting.note: Plant bare-root while dormant in late winter; a mid-season Korean-bred nashi cultivar and needs a different Asian pear cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Whangkeumbae was released to Korean orchards by the national horticultural research institute and has since become a widely grown commercial cultivar valued for its high sugar content and attractive yellowish-green skin at harvest. The flesh is crisp and juicy, eaten fresh at full ripeness rather than softened in storage the way European pears are. It requires a compatible cross-pollinator and, as with most nashi cultivars, offers limited natural resistance to fire blight.
sources: ISHS — Achievements of Pear Breeding in Korea

planting.note: Plant bare-root while dormant in late winter; bred in Japan as a more productive replacement for the early-ripening Shinsui cultivar and blooms and ripens a few days later than Shinsui, in a window close to Kosui. Plant with a different Asian pear cultivar for cross-pollination.

directions: Chikusui produces orange-russeted fruit with yellowish-white flesh that is soft-crisp and juicy, with a firmness close to Kosui and slightly higher than Hosui, eaten fresh rather than stored to soften. It was developed specifically to improve on the productivity problems of the earlier Shinsui cultivar while keeping a similarly early harvest window. It requires a compatible cross-pollinator and shares the general fire blight susceptibility common to nashi pears.
